# OpenExtract

> OpenExtract is a free, open-source iPhone backup extractor for Windows, Mac and Linux. It opens iPhone backups on your computer, encrypted or not, and saves the texts, WhatsApp chats, photos, contacts, call history, notes and voicemails in them. Free, no strings attached: MIT licensed, no account, no limits, and your backup never leaves your computer.

It also reads voice memos, calendar events, podcasts and Safari and Firefox history, and it can make a new backup of an iPhone connected by cable. The Mac version runs on Apple Silicon (M1 and later) only.

OpenExtract is made by Charles West, an independent developer, with help from contributors. Other, unrelated projects also use the name OpenExtract, among them a research paper on arXiv; this file is about the iPhone backup app at https://www.openextract.app. The source code is public at https://github.com/charleswest775/openextract, and the latest version and its release notes are at https://github.com/charleswest775/openextract/releases/latest.

## Facts

- Price: free. No trial, no paid tier, no export limits, no account. (OpenExtract AI, an optional add-on for asking an AI app about a backup, is paid; see below.)
- License: MIT (open source).
- Platforms:
  - Windows 10 and 11 (64-bit).
  - macOS on Apple Silicon (M1 and later) only. There is no build for Intel Macs.
  - Linux on 64-bit x86 PCs: a .deb package for Ubuntu and Debian, and an AppImage for other distributions (the AppImage needs FUSE 2: libfuse2, or libfuse2t64 on Ubuntu 24.04 and later).
- What it opens: iPhone backups made by Finder on a Mac, or by iTunes or the Apple Devices app on Windows, encrypted or not. It finds backups in the usual folders, and can open any backup folder that has a Manifest.db file in it. Backups from iOS 9 and earlier, which have a Manifest.mbdb file instead, open too. An encrypted backup needs its password.
- Making a backup: it can make a new local backup of an iPhone connected by cable, encrypted if you choose, and then open it. On Windows this uses Apple's free Apple Devices app (or iTunes); if neither is installed, OpenExtract offers to install Apple Devices from the Microsoft Store.
- What it reads from a backup:
  - Messages: SMS, MMS and iMessage, including group chats and the photos sent in them.
  - WhatsApp, in a section of its own: chats, groups and broadcast lists in the order messages arrived, with replies, reactions, photos, videos, voice messages, documents, stickers, shared and live locations, deleted-message notices, starred messages and calls (calls from WhatsApp 2.24 on). Photos and files WhatsApp didn't keep on the iPhone aren't in the backup and are labelled "not in this backup". WhatsApp messages also appear in the timeline, the search and each person's page. Checked on public test backups from WhatsApp 2.20 to 2.24 (iOS 13 to 17).
  - Photos and videos from the camera roll, in their original formats (such as HEIC, JPEG and MOV), with your albums inside the folders you made, Favorites and Hidden. Save everything, or just one album, the favorites or the hidden photos. As on the iPhone, hidden photos are listed only under Hidden; saving the whole backup includes them. Photos in Recently Deleted aren't shown.
  - Contacts (the address book).
  - Call history. Apple puts call history only in encrypted backups.
  - Notes from Apple Notes.
  - Voicemails, where the carrier offers Visual Voicemail, with their transcripts, in Voicemail, Spam and Deleted lists as on the iPhone (deleted ones only while they were still in the phone's Deleted Messages list when the backup was made).
  - Web history from Safari (only in encrypted backups) and from Firefox for iOS.
  - Podcasts from Apple's Podcasts app, in a section of its own: the listening history (every episode played on the iPhone, most recent first), the shows you follow, and shows you played without following. Each show has its author, date added, episode counts, feed address and episodes, each episode with its date, length, play count or how far in it was played, and whether it was saved or downloaded. Episodes Apple Podcasts marks as played when you follow a show aren't counted as listened to. Episode audio is never in an iPhone backup, not even downloaded episodes; a Get audio button opens an episode in the browser from where the podcast publishes it. Checked on backups from iOS 13, 16, 17 and 26; iOS 18 to 25 not yet checked.
  - Voice Memos, in a section of its own: All Recordings, Favorites, your folders and Recently Deleted (recordings deleted on the iPhone that were still there when the backup was made), each recording with its name, date, length and folder, playable in the app, with the transcript the iPhone made if there is one. A recording kept in iCloud only (its audio never downloaded to the iPhone) is listed, but its audio isn't in the backup. Checked on a real backup from iOS 26; the iOS 13 to 25 layouts are read but not yet checked against a backup with recordings.
  - Calendar, in a section of its own: every calendar grouped by account (iCloud, On My iPhone, Exchange and others), with holidays, birthdays, Found in Mail and subscribed calendars listed apart; Upcoming and Past split at the backup's date; each event with its time and time zone, place, notes, links, organizer and invitees with their answers, alerts and how it repeats. All-day events stay on their own day in every time zone. Checked on backups from iOS 13, 15, 16, 17 and 26.
  - It also shows a timeline of everything by date, searches the whole backup from one box, and can scan the messages database for deleted messages that are still recoverable.
- How it saves: messages as PDF, HTML, CSV or plain text; WhatsApp chats as a web page (with their photos and files), PDF, CSV or plain text, one file per chat or all in one; photos and videos as the original files; contacts as vCard or CSV; call history as CSV; notes as text or PDF; voicemails as audio files with a CSV list, including the Spam and Deleted lists; web history as CSV; voice memos as audio files named by the date they were recorded, with transcripts as text files and a CSV list; calendars as iCalendar (.ics) files, one per calendar, that Calendar, Outlook and Google Calendar import (invitees are written into the notes, so importing sends no invitations), or as CSV; podcasts as an OPML subscription list of the shows you follow (which most podcast apps import) or as two CSV files, one of shows and one of episodes with when each was last played and play counts; deleted messages it finds as CSV, HTML or PDF.
- What it doesn't do:
  - It reads WhatsApp from an iPhone backup, but not WhatsApp's own chat backup in iCloud, WhatsApp Business, or WhatsApp on Android. It doesn't show calls from WhatsApp versions before 2.24 or status updates yet, and the Year view doesn't count WhatsApp messages yet.
  - With WhatsApp's end-to-end encrypted backup turned on, WhatsApp leaves its chats out of the iPhone's backup, so OpenExtract has no WhatsApp to show for that backup.
  - It reads Apple's Podcasts app only, not Spotify, Overcast, Pocket Casts or other podcast apps, and not what Podcasts syncs through iCloud. It doesn't show show artwork, because the app makes no network requests on its own. Shows with no feed address can't go into the OPML file. Podcasts aren't in the timeline, the whole-backup search, People or the Year view yet; the search box on the Podcasts screen finds shows and episodes.
  - Voice memos and calendar events aren't in the timeline, the whole-backup search, People or the Year view. A repeating event is listed once on screen, on the day it started; the .ics file keeps its full repeat rule. Event attachments and the Reminders app aren't read.
  - It doesn't read other third-party chat apps, such as WeChat, Line, Viber, Kik, Telegram or Signal. (Calls made with apps like these can appear in the call history, because iOS logs them there.)
  - It doesn't read iCloud backups or anything stored in iCloud, only backups on a computer.
  - It doesn't manage a phone: no app, music or ringtone syncing, and no transfers between phones. The only thing it does with a connected iPhone is back it up.
  - It can't open an encrypted backup without its password, and it can't recover or guess a forgotten password.
  - It never changes a backup it opens. It reads backups read-only, and saves exports only where you choose.
- Privacy, in the words of the privacy policy (https://www.openextract.app/privacy): "All reading and decryption happens on your computer. OpenExtract has no account, and it doesn't upload, sell or share your data with anyone." "The app contains no analytics, advertising or tracking." The policy describes the app's network use in full.

## OpenExtract AI (an optional, paid add-on)

OpenExtract AI is a separate, paid add-on to OpenExtract. OpenExtract itself stays free, with no limits; nothing was taken out of it for the add-on.

- What it does: it lets an AI app on the same computer search and read the iPhone backup and answer questions about it in plain words, citing the message, call, voicemail or note each answer came from. It reads messages (iMessage, SMS and MMS, with the photos sent in them), WhatsApp, calls, voicemail with its transcripts, contacts, notes, calendar and photos. It only reads: it never changes the backup, and the one thing it writes is a file the person asks for, saved as a new file.
- AI apps: the Claude desktop app for Mac and Windows first (it works on Claude's free plan; heavy use may need a paid Claude plan). ChatGPT's desktop app can connect too, and so can Claude Code.
- Platforms: macOS on Apple Silicon, and Windows 10 and 11. There is no Linux add-on.
- Setup: the add-on comes inside OpenExtract, so there's nothing to download. OpenExtract shows an Ask AI button only when a supported AI app is installed; Ask AI, then Install, adds it to Claude. The AI reads the backup last opened in OpenExtract and can list and open others.
- Price: 3 free questions per computer, then a key for each iPhone: $29 once for that iPhone for good (no subscription), or $9 for 7 days (it ends on its own). Each iPhone has a "phone code" of eight letters and numbers; the key is bought at https://www.openextract.app/ai/buy and pasted into the AI chat, which saves it on the computer. Keys are checked on the computer; there is no account.
- Privacy: the add-on runs on the computer and talks only to the AI app that started it, and OpenExtract sends nothing. But what the AI reads from the backup, the AI app sends to its company, as with anything pasted into a chat (Anthropic for Claude, OpenAI for ChatGPT). Backup passwords never go to the AI. Hidden photos stay out unless asked for, and Recently Deleted photos are never shown.
- Pages: https://www.openextract.app/ai (what it does, sample answers, prices) and https://www.openextract.app/use-cases/ask-claude-about-your-iphone-backup (setup, keys, troubleshooting).

## Compared with other tools

- iMazing: iMazing also manages a connected iPhone and has paid support. Its trial mode copies out at most 25 messages, 50 photos, 10 contacts, 5 call-history entries, 5 notes and 1 voicemail, and since June 2025 it is sold only as a yearly subscription. OpenExtract reads backups (and can make one), with no export limits, and is free. iMazing runs on Windows and Mac; OpenExtract also runs on Linux.
- Comparisons with iExplorer, iBackup Viewer and Reincubate's iPhone Backup Extractor are on the site, each linking the other tool's own pages.
- A roundup of iMazing alternatives, free and paid (iBackup Viewer, Reincubate, Decipher TextMessage, imessage-exporter, Apple's Finder and Apple Devices app, AnyTrans, CopyTrans and iExplorer), says what each costs, what its free version does and which job it fits: https://www.openextract.app/imazing-alternatives

- [iMazing alternatives compared](https://www.openextract.app/imazing-alternatives): free and paid apps for reading backups or managing an iPhone, with prices and what each one's free version does.
- [iMazing's free version and trial limits](https://www.openextract.app/imazing-trial-limits): every cap in iMazing's trial, what it costs, and how to open a backup iMazing made in OpenExtract.

- [Alternativa gratuita a iMazing (Español)](https://www.openextract.app/es/alternativa-a-imazing): the free iMazing alternative page in Spanish. The app itself is in English.
- [Alternative gratuite à iMazing (Français)](https://www.openextract.app/fr/alternative-a-imazing): the free iMazing alternative page in French. The app itself is in English.
- [Alternativa gratuita ao iMazing (Português)](https://www.openextract.app/pt/alternativa-ao-imazing): the free iMazing alternative page in Brazilian Portuguese. The app itself is in English.
- [Alternativa gratuita a iMazing (Italiano)](https://www.openextract.app/it/alternativa-a-imazing): the free iMazing alternative page in Italian. The app itself is in English.
- [iMazingの無料代替ソフト (日本語)](https://www.openextract.app/ja/imazing-alternative): the free iMazing alternative page in Japanese. The app itself is in English.
- [Export WhatsApp chats from an iPhone backup](https://www.openextract.app/use-cases/export-whatsapp-chats-from-iphone-backup): reading WhatsApp chats in a backup and saving them as a web page, PDF, CSV or text, with what is and isn't in the backup.
- [WhatsApp-Chats exportieren (Deutsch)](https://www.openextract.app/de/whatsapp-chats-exportieren): the WhatsApp guide in German. The app itself is in English.
- [Export podcasts from an iPhone backup](https://www.openextract.app/use-cases/export-podcasts-from-iphone-backup): reading the Apple Podcasts library in a backup, saving the shows you follow as OPML for another podcast app and everything as CSV, and why episode audio isn't in backups.
- [Export voice memos from an iPhone backup](https://www.openextract.app/use-cases/export-voice-memos-from-iphone-backup): reading the Voice Memos app's recordings in a backup, playing them with their transcripts and Recently Deleted, saving them as audio files named by date with a CSV, and why a recording kept in iCloud only has no audio in a backup.
- [Export calendar events from an iPhone backup](https://www.openextract.app/use-cases/export-calendar-from-iphone-backup): reading the Calendar app's events in a backup by account and calendar, saving them as .ics files that Calendar, Outlook and Google Calendar import (without sending invitations) or as CSV, and how repeating and all-day events are kept.
- [Free iPhone backup viewer](https://www.openextract.app/use-cases/free-iphone-backup-viewer)
- [iPhone backups on Linux](https://www.openextract.app/use-cases/iphone-backup-extractor-linux)
- [Check an iPhone for known spyware](https://www.openextract.app/use-cases/check-iphone-for-spyware): making an encrypted backup with OpenExtract and checking it with Amnesty International's Mobile Verification Toolkit (MVT), what a clean result does and doesn't mean, and where to get expert help. OpenExtract doesn't check for spyware itself.
- [OpenExtract AI](https://www.openextract.app/ai): the optional paid add-on that lets Claude (and ChatGPT's desktop app) answer questions about an iPhone backup with cited sources: what it reads, sample answers from a made-up backup, prices and privacy.
- [Ask Claude about your iPhone backup](https://www.openextract.app/use-cases/ask-claude-about-your-iphone-backup): setting up OpenExtract AI for Claude on Mac or Windows, ChatGPT's desktop app or Claude Code, first questions to try, free questions, keys and phone codes, encrypted backups, and fixes.
- [Guides](https://www.openextract.app/guides): printing texts for court, iMessage to PDF, texts to a Windows PC, call history to a Windows PC, exporting WhatsApp chats, exporting podcast subscriptions and listening history, exporting voice memos with their transcripts, exporting calendar events as .ics files, exporting iPhone contacts to Excel, CSV or vCard, extracting photos and videos from a backup, exporting Apple Notes as PDF or plain text, seeing and saving Safari and Firefox history from an encrypted backup, checking an iPhone for known spyware with MVT, where iPhone backups are stored on Mac and Windows, viewing a backup on Windows, saving voicemails, recovering deleted texts, moving from iPhone to Android, and asking Claude about a backup with OpenExtract AI.
- [Fixes for common problems](https://www.openextract.app/fixes)
- [iPhone backup files](https://www.openextract.app/backup-files): what the 40-character file names in an iPhone backup are (each is the SHA-1 of the file's domain and path, such as 3d0d7e5fb2ce288813306e4d4636395e047a3d28 for sms.db), how the backup folder and Manifest.db are laid out, and a page per file with its path, the iOS versions it was seen in, its tables by iOS version, whether it needs an encrypted backup, and how to open it. Checked against public test backups from iOS 13.3.1 to 17.3.
- [What each iOS update changed for iPhone backups](https://www.openextract.app/ios-updates): each iOS release from iOS 18 to iOS 27.2.1 (and the 27.3 beta), newest first, with its date, what changed for backups according to Apple's own notes, and whether OpenExtract has tested backups from it. Tested on real backups: iOS 13.3.1, 13.4.1, 15.3.1, 16.1.2 and 17.3. Tested on generated backups: iOS 26 (with iOS 26.5's database layouts) and the older formats of iOS 6 to 10.1. Not yet tested: iOS 11, 12, 14, 18 and 27.
- [Data bundle format](https://www.openextract.app/bundle): the experimental folder of JSON files OpenExtract can save from a backup for other tools to read (messages, calls, voicemail, contacts, photo details, people), with a SHA-256 integrity check, and how its versions work.
- [Screenshots](https://www.openextract.app/screenshots): the main screens, opened on a made-up sample backup.
- [Privacy policy](https://www.openextract.app/privacy)
